title: Redwood discovery - model selection - Pelorus AI
summary: Initial discovery focused on model selection for Pelorus AI's multilingual customer support assistant. Key constraints: long context for conversation history (~200k tokens across sessions but 32k window desired), strong multilingual support (EN/ES/PT), tool-calling for internal ticketing + KB search, and enterprise security (SSO, KMS, audit logs). Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs and agreed next steps: Redwood to share pricing/TCO, security docs, and run a focused latency/quality benchmark with their prompt set.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Malhotra (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Pelorus CTO), Devon Lee (ML Eng), Sanjay Rao (Infra), Aisha Khan (Product)

[00:00] Jared: Hey everybody, thanks for joining — Jared Kim from Redwood, AE on the call. Priya from our SE team is here, she'll do the deep than the deep technical run. How's everyone doing?
[00:15] Marta: Doing good, thanks. Busy but excited to dig in.
[00:22] Priya: Hi all, quick agenda — understand your model selection needs, context and multilingual, tool-calling requirements, security constraints, then propose options Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private and next steps.
[00:35] Devon: Great. For context, Pelorus is building a conversational assistant embedded in our support UI, must handle Spanish, Portuguese and English. Latency needs are sub 1s for partial streaming for short queries, and we also need really long context for multi-turn threads — think 50k–200k tokens of conversation history but realistically want a 32k window for active context.
[01:05] Jared: Makes sense. When you say 50k–200k across sessions, are you planning to bring the full history in every request or use a retrieval approach?
[01:13] Devon: We'd stitch a compacted history — but sometimes we need long-range recall — like earlier transcripts and attachments. Also tool calls to our ticketing system and KB search.
[01:22] Priya: Okay right. So two constraints — long active context window and tool-calling with structured outputs. Redwood supports model variants that do function/tool calling patterns, and we can route to models that have stronger structured output guarantees. For long context, we have a couple levers: models with native extended context (32k, 64k), KV-cache prefix caching, and our cache-aware batching so you don't pay huge per-token costs for repeated context.
[01:50] Sanjay: Quick Q — we run in Azure with private networking; can we do VPC peering if we go Dedicated or Private? Also keys — KMS required.
[01:58] Priya: Yes. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with VPC connectivity and Redwood Private gives your full control — private control plane or on‑prem. We integrate with customer KMS/HSMs and support audit logs and SAML/SSO. We'll share the exact diagrams.
[02:15] Marta: Security is a big checkbox. Are you SOC2 + ISO? We need vendor attestation to pass procurement.
[02:22] Jared: Redwood is SOC2 Type II, and we can provide the report under NDA — we'll attach in the security pack.
[02:30] Devon: On models themselves, curious about open models vs proprietary ones. We prefer open models for auditability and licensing. Which open models do you recommend for multilingual + tool calling?
[02:40] Priya: We often recommend a shortlist by use case. For multilingual and tool-calling we see good results with a few families — Llama3-series forks, Mistral variants, and some of the larger Llama2-derived or RedWood-verified open models. For heavy multi-lingual QA Portuguese/Spanish, Mistral-large-ish and some tuned Llama forks do well. Also need to consider quantization and perf on your infra.
[03:10] Devon: Are there models that natively support function calling like OpenAI? We need reliable structured JSON outputs for our ticket payloads.
[03:17] Priya: Some open models don't have explicit "function calling" protocol, but you can enforce structured output via strong prompt templates and schema-guided decoding. We also provide a tool-calling shim in the hosted API that helps convert model outputs into typed payloads and validates them before calling the downstream API. For Dedicated/Private you can run that shim inside your network or use the Redwood control plane.
[03:45] Aisha: Latency — you mentioned sub-1s partial streaming, what's realistic on Hosted vs Dedicated?
[03:52] Jared: For short single-turn queries, Hosted models on our managed endpoints can hit median <200ms token latency for small models; larger context and bigger models push that up. Dedicated lets you provision GPUs for predictable p99 latency and reduced jitter; Private gives you the lowest network hops if you colocate. We can share benchmark numbers against your prompt set.
[04:15] Sanjay: How does batching affect latency for interactive sessions?
[04:20] Priya: We do adaptive batching — interactive sessions get lower batching and priority routing to meet latency SLOs. Batching is more aggressive for async workloads. Also intelligent caching of prefixes helps reduce work for repeated context. There's a tradeoff: you can favor cost (bigger batches) or latency (smaller batches).
[04:40] Marta: Cost-wise we want a rough TCO: Hosted per-token vs Dedicated reserved monthly. We expect high query volumes.
[04:48] Jared: We'll send a TCO worksheet. Typical pattern — start hosted for evaluation + low-latency features, then move to Dedicated as volume grows; some customers go Private for compliance. We'll model your qps, average response lengths and caching to show breakeven.
[05:05] Devon: On quality regressions — we need guardrails, monitoring, and eval tooling.
[05:10] Priya: Redwood Optimize has eval and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. You can run continuous evals and we can trigger rollbacks or automatic fallback to a safe model variant. Also token-level cost breakdowns in the Console.
[05:26] Marta: For multilingual, any examples of metrics or benchmarks?
[05:30] Priya: We can run a short multilingual bench using your sample utterances. We typically compare accuracy/intent extraction and hallucination rates across candidate open models and a reference closed model.
[05:42] Devon: For long-context, is the KV cache completely transparent? We worry about cold starts when a session hasn't been seen before.
[05:50] Priya: Cold starts are real — our approach is warm caches for high-frequency prefixes and we also support persistent session caches for Dedicated/Private, which reduces cold start penalties. For Hosted, aggressive prefix compaction reduces bandwidth. We'll demonstrate with your dataset.
[06:10] Sanjay: Operational questions: how are upgrades, rollouts handled? We need canary and A/B testing.
[06:18] Priya: Rollouts are supported — canary, A/B, automatic fallback policies, and routing by policy (latency/cost/region). The Console surfaces per-model rollouts and tracing for requests.
[06:30] Marta: Procurement — do you have standard enterprise terms? Data residency?
[06:35] Jared: Yes, we have enterprise contracts and can add data residency clauses; Private gives the most control. We'll flag the standard MSA template in the follow-up.
[06:45] [Pause / notes exchanged]
[07:00] Devon: For the bench we're proposing, can we include tool-calling scenarios with a simulated ticket API and KB retrieval?
[07:08] Priya: Absolutely, include the ticket payload examples and we can validate structured outputs. We'll also run models with and without strong decoding constraints to show differences.
[07:18] Devon: One more technical — are there any limitations on context window when using quantized models or lower-precision kernels?
[07:24] Priya: Good question. Quantization itself doesn't always reduce context length, but some optimized execution paths have tradeoffs in performance. For example, some 4-bit kernels are faster but may limit certain runtimes for 64k context; kernel selection happens at compile time per model and hardware. We'll surface recommended quantization profiles per model.
[07:45] Jared: Any red flags from procurement side, Marta?
[07:50] Marta: Nothing major yet, just need SOC2, SSO compatibility and the security diagram. Also curious about offline/on-prem possibilities for certain regulated customers.
[07:58] Priya: For on-prem we do a packaged Private deployment with customer-managed control plane and optional air-gapped installs. We document KMS/HSM integration and audit log ingestion.
[08:10] Sanjay: Networking — will we need to open a lot of ports for Dedicated?
[08:15] Priya: We provide network diagrams; usually it's standard egress to Redwood control plane plus optional private peering. We'll include exact port lists in the security pack.
[08:25] [Summary recap by Jared]
[08:30] Jared: Quick recap — main asks: 1) multilang + long-context model shortlist, 2) tool-calling reliability for ticketing, 3) security pack (SOC2, KMS, SSO & network), 4) TCO worksheet for Hosted vs Dedicated, 5) bench run with their prompt sets. We'll send those docs asap and schedule the follow-up tech deep-dive.
[08:52] Marta: Sounds good. On timing, we hope to choose a path within 4–6 weeks.
[08:58] Jared: Great — we'll aim to have all deliverables in 1 week and bench planned the following week.
[09:05] Devon: One tiny nit — when you say "Redwood-verified" models, what does that verification cover?
[09:12] Priya: We run performance profiles (latency, throughput), quality checks on evals, and safety/regression scans. We publish verified performance profiles in the model catalog.
[09:24] Marta: Any internal references of companies doing similar multilingual long-context apps?
[09:29] Jared: We can share anonymized case studies — some customers in fintech and ecommerce use similar setups. We'll include a small reference list.
[09:40] Aisha: For the bench, we need to include attachments (like small logs). Can Redwood handle multi-part inputs?
[09:46] Priya: Yes, you can attach base64 blobs or provide retrieval references; we often use KB retrieval + doc embeddings for attachments. For privacy, we can run it in Dedicated/Private.
[09:58] [Wrap up]
[10:05] Jared: Thanks everyone — action items as noted. We'll follow up with the security pack and TCO.
[10:12] Marta: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript. Notes: transcription shows small name misspellings and occasional words like "KV cash" in earlier auto notes; speakers were mostly correctly labeled but occasional system labelling may happen in raw export.
